fhb-low-deposit.html: Buying a first home without a full 20% deposit is more common than many buyers expect. In September 2026, just over half of all first-home mortgages approved across New Zealand (50.3%—1,342 of 2,667 loans, or $850m in lending) went to buyers with under a 20% deposit, up from 46.0% a year earlier.
fhb-low-deposit.source_html: Source: RBNZ Table C31, © Reserve Bank of New Zealand. Percentages & averages derived by HLF. Historical market statistics for general information only, not personalised financial advice.

fhb-share.html: First-home buyers continue to make up an active slice of the New Zealand market—in September 2026, banks approved 2,667 first-home mortgages (20.3% of all new mortgage lending, up from 19.2% a year earlier), with an average loan size of $574k.
fhb-share.source_html: Source: RBNZ Table C31, © Reserve Bank of New Zealand. Percentages & averages derived by HLF. Historical market statistics for general information only, not personalised financial advice.

investors.html: First-home buyers are currently borrowing more overall than property investors—in September 2026, investors made up 17.7% of new mortgage lending ($1.33B, down from 21.2% a year earlier), compared with 20.3% for first-home buyers.
investors.source_html: Source: RBNZ Table C31, © Reserve Bank of New Zealand. Percentages & averages derived by HLF. Historical market statistics for general information only, not personalised financial advice.

refinance.html: Moving banks is a regular part of the New Zealand mortgage market rather than a rare step—in September 2026 alone, 2,772 borrowers switched mortgage providers, moving $1.73B in loans (23.0% of all new lending, at an average loan size of $624k).
refinance.source_html: Source: RBNZ Table C33, © Reserve Bank of New Zealand. Derived by HLF. Historical market statistics for general information only, not personalised financial advice.

top-ups.html: Many Kiwi homeowners tap into existing equity for renovations or upgrades rather than moving house—in September 2026, 9,639 borrowers topped up an existing mortgage, making up 46.4% of all mortgage approvals by count (average top-up: $100k).
top-ups.source_html: Source: RBNZ Table C33, © Reserve Bank of New Zealand. Derived by HLF. Historical market statistics for general information only, not personalised financial advice.

settled-rates.html: Advertised bank rates only tell half the story—across all new fixed mortgages actually settled in September 2026, New Zealand borrowers locked in a weighted-average rate of 4.82% for one year and 5.09% for two years.
settled-rates.source_html: Source: RBNZ Table B30, © Reserve Bank of New Zealand. Historical market statistics for general information only.

rent-yield-pulse.html: Private weekly rents across New Zealand have been relatively steady over the past year—the national median sat at $595/wk in August 2026 (up 0.8% on a year earlier), with regional medians at $650/wk in Auckland, $580/wk in Wellington, and $550/wk in Canterbury.
rent-yield-pulse.source_html: Source: Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (Tenancy Services Rental Bond Data), licensed under CC BY 3.0 NZ. Derived by HLF. Historical market statistics only.

rental-bonds-supply.html: Thousands of New Zealand households sign new leases every month—Tenancy Services logged 13,062 newly lodged private rental bonds in August 2026, across a nationwide pool of 522,942 active private tenancies.
rental-bonds-supply.source_html: Source: Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (Tenancy Services Rental Bond Data), licensed under CC BY 3.0 NZ. Derived by HLF. Historical market statistics only.

student-loan-servicing.html: Student debt is a familiar line item on home loan applications—across Inland Revenue's June 2026 figures, the median NZ student loan balance sat at $18,301 (up 4.5% on a year earlier), where compulsory PAYE deductions factor into how banks test monthly servicing.
student-loan-servicing.source_html: Source: Inland Revenue — Student Loan Statistics (Jun 2026), licensed under CC BY 4.0. Servicing context by HLF for general information only.

kiwisaver-first-home.html: For many buyers, KiwiSaver does much of the heavy lifting toward a first deposit—in September 2026, 4,250 members withdrew a combined $195.7m to put toward a first home—averaging ~$46k per withdrawing member, or roughly $73k of KiwiSaver funds per approved first-home mortgage.
kiwisaver-first-home.source_html: Source: Inland Revenue — KiwiSaver Withdrawal Statistics cross-referenced with RBNZ Table C31, licensed under CC BY 4.0. Derived by HLF for general information only.

kiwisaver-switches.html: Reviewing and changing KiwiSaver providers happens more regularly than many members realise—over the year to June 2026, 198,897 New Zealanders moved their balance to a new scheme, averaging 16,575 switches every month.
kiwisaver-switches.source_html: Source: Inland Revenue — KiwiSaver Scheme Transfer Statistics (CC BY 4.0). Monthly average derived by HLF. General information only, not personalised KiwiSaver advice.

new-builds-annual.html: New-build supply across New Zealand has been gathering pace, with 41,091 new homes consented in the year to September 2026 (up 18.0% on the previous year, including 3,570 dwellings consented in September 2026).
new-builds-annual.source_html: Source: Stats NZ — Building Consents Issued (September 2026), licensed under CC BY 4.0. Multi-unit share derived by HLF. Historical market statistics only.

townhouse-share.html: Townhouses and multi-unit developments now make up more than half of new residential consents—accounting for 51.5% (1,837 of 3,570 homes) consented in September 2026, including 1,305 townhouses, flats, and units.
townhouse-share.source_html: Source: Stats NZ — Building Consents Issued (September 2026), licensed under CC BY 4.0. Multi-unit share derived by HLF. Historical market statistics only.

build-cost-inflation.html: Residential build-cost inflation has settled into single digits compared with the post-pandemic construction surge—Stats NZ recorded a +3.2% annual change in the cost of purchasing a newly built home in the September 2026 quarter, alongside 3.7% overall CPI inflation.
build-cost-inflation.source_html: Source: Stats NZ — Consumers Price Index (September 2026 quarter), licensed under CC BY 4.0. Historical market statistics only.

interest-only.html: Loan structures look quite different between rental properties and family homes in the Reserve Bank figures—in September 2026, 31.5% of new investor lending was set up on interest-only terms (including revolving credit), compared with 13.7% for owner-occupiers.
interest-only.source_html: Source: RBNZ Table C32, © Reserve Bank of New Zealand. Derived by HLF. Historical market statistics for general information only, not personalised financial advice.

dti-headroom.html: Most first-home lending currently sits well inside the Reserve Bank's Debt-to-Income limits—in September 2026, 9.1% of first-home buyer lending had a DTI ratio above 6x, sitting 10.9 percentage points below RBNZ's 20% bank speed-limit allowance.
dti-headroom.source_html: Source: RBNZ Table C40, © Reserve Bank of New Zealand. Derived by HLF. Historical market statistics for general information only.

fhb-loan-size-gap.html: First-home buyers with under a 20% deposit actually take out larger mortgages on average ($633,383) than buyers with a 20%+ deposit ($513,208)—a $120,175 difference in September 2026, as higher-earning couples often use a 10%–15% deposit to buy sooner rather than renting for extra years to save 20%.
fhb-loan-size-gap.source_html: Source: RBNZ Table C31, © Reserve Bank of New Zealand. Percentages & averages derived by HLF. Historical market statistics for general information only, not personalised financial advice.

fhb-bank-lvr-priority.html: When New Zealand banks approve low-deposit mortgages (>80% LVR), most of their allowance goes to first-home buyers. In September 2026, 67.2% of all low-deposit mortgage dollars ($850m of $1.26B) and 62.0% of low-deposit loans (1,342 of 2,165) went directly to first-home buyers.
fhb-bank-lvr-priority.source_html: Source: RBNZ Table C31, © Reserve Bank of New Zealand. Percentages & averages derived by HLF. Historical market statistics for general information only, not personalised financial advice.

fhb-20-deposit-club.html: Crossing the 20% deposit mark unlocks sharp advertised bank special rates and avoids low-equity margins. In September 2026, 1,325 first-home buyers (49.7% of approvals, or $680m) bought with a 20%+ deposit, borrowing an average of $513,208.
fhb-20-deposit-club.source_html: Source: RBNZ Table C31, © Reserve Bank of New Zealand. Percentages & averages derived by HLF. Historical market statistics for general information only, not personalised financial advice.

fhb-vs-investors.html: First-home buyers are out-borrowing property investors across New Zealand. In September 2026, banks approved $1.53B (20.3% of lending) for first-home buyers compared with $1.33B (17.7%) for property investors—putting first-home buyers $195m ahead.
fhb-vs-investors.source_html: Source: RBNZ Table C31, © Reserve Bank of New Zealand. Percentages & averages derived by HLF. Historical market statistics for general information only, not personalised financial advice.

owner-equity-buffer.html: Most existing Kiwi homeowners hold more usable equity than they realise. In September 2026, 94.9% of existing owner-occupier mortgages approved across New Zealand (14,327 of 15,096 loans, or $4.16B) had at least 20% equity, carrying an average loan size of $290,082.
owner-equity-buffer.source_html: Source: RBNZ Table C31, © Reserve Bank of New Zealand. Percentages & averages derived by HLF. Historical market statistics for general information only, not personalised financial advice.

investor-equity-tiers.html: You don't need 40% equity locked up to buy an investment property. In September 2026, 43.8% of approved NZ property investors had 40%+ equity—while 36.4% bought in the 30%–40% equity band and 19.8% (527 loans, or $337m) were approved with under 30% equity.
investor-equity-tiers.source_html: Source: RBNZ Table C31, © Reserve Bank of New Zealand. Percentages & averages derived by HLF. Historical market statistics for general information only, not personalised financial advice.

mover-low-equity.html: Low-deposit lending isn't restricted to first-home buyers. In September 2026, New Zealand banks approved 769 mortgages ($378m) for existing owner-occupiers moving or borrowing with under 20% equity (>80% LVR)—accounting for 5.1% of existing homeowner approvals, up from 3.3% a year earlier.
mover-low-equity.source_html: Source: RBNZ Table C31, © Reserve Bank of New Zealand. Percentages & averages derived by HLF. Historical market statistics for general information only, not personalised financial advice.

fhb-annual-milestone.html: Over the 12 months to September 2026, New Zealand banks approved 33,485 first-home buyer mortgages totalling $19.61B in lending (up from 31,589 loans a year earlier)—including 15,743 buyers (47.0%) who bought with under a 20% deposit.
fhb-annual-milestone.source_html: Source: RBNZ Table C31, © Reserve Bank of New Zealand. Percentages & averages derived by HLF. Historical market statistics for general information only, not personalised financial advice.

equity-topup-demand.html: Tapping into home equity without selling is one of the most common moves in New Zealand banking—in September 2026, homeowners unlocked $962m in mortgage top-ups across 9,639 existing properties (averaging $100k per top-up) for renovations, debt consolidation, and investment deposits.
equity-topup-demand.source_html: Source: RBNZ Table C33, © Reserve Bank of New Zealand. Derived by HLF. Historical market statistics for general information only, not personalised financial advice.

investor-vs-owner-io.html: Loan structures look quite different between rental properties and family homes in the Reserve Bank figures—in September 2026, 31.5% of new investor lending was set up on interest-only terms (including revolving credit), compared with 13.7% for owner-occupiers.
investor-vs-owner-io.source_html: Source: RBNZ Table C32, © Reserve Bank of New Zealand. Derived by HLF. Historical market statistics for general information only, not personalised financial advice.

borrower-income.html: Because mortgage applications often combine two incomes, approved first-home buyers in September 2026 recorded an average gross borrower income of $144.2k nationwide.
borrower-income.source_html: Source: RBNZ Table C41, © Reserve Bank of New Zealand. Derived by HLF for general information only.

fhb-income-akl-vs-nz.html: Because most first-home applications combine two incomes, approved first-home buyers in September 2026 averaged $144,232 in combined pre-tax income nationwide—though single-income buyers regularly qualify using regional price points, boarder income, or Kāinga Ora support.
fhb-income-akl-vs-nz.source_html: Source: RBNZ Table C41, © Reserve Bank of New Zealand. Derived by HLF for general information only.

fhb-regional-kiwisaver.html: Pooling two KiwiSaver accounts is how most Kiwi couples build their deposit—over the year to June 2026, 50,330 first-home buyers withdrew $2.27B from KiwiSaver, averaging $45,005 per person nationwide (~$90,000 per couple), led by Wellington ($50,364/person) and Auckland ($47,630/person).
fhb-regional-kiwisaver.source_html: Source: Inland Revenue — KiwiSaver Fund Withdrawals by Region (Year ended Jun 2026), licensed under CC BY 4.0. Per-member averages derived by HLF for general information only.

kiwisaver-active-switchers.html: Reviewing and changing KiwiSaver providers happens more regularly than many members realise—over the year to June 2026, 198,897 New Zealanders moved their balance to a new scheme, averaging 16,575 switches every month.
kiwisaver-active-switchers.source_html: Source: Inland Revenue — KiwiSaver Scheme Transfer Statistics (CC BY 4.0). Monthly average derived by HLF. General information only, not personalised KiwiSaver advice.
